lessons.title: Lesson 1: Why a nonprofit needs an AI plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain to your board or leadership why your organization needs a simple AI plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given your organization's mission, you will explain to your board or leadership why your organization needs a simple AI plan, starting from the mission, not the tool.
Your staff and volunteers may already be using AI tools on their own, with no shared rules. That can save time, but it can also put donor or client information at risk or produce writing that does not sound like you.
An AI plan is a short document that says what AI is for in your organization, what it is not for, who decides, and how you will check that it helps your mission.
A good plan starts with the mission, not the tool. The question is not "Which AI should we buy?" but "Where does our team lose time that could go back to the people we serve?"
Words to know:
- AI plan: a short document saying how your organization will and will not use AI.
- Mission: the purpose your organization exists to serve.
- Stakeholder: anyone affected by your work: clients, donors, volunteers, staff, board.
Try it now: Write your mission in one sentence at the top of a blank page titled "Our AI Plan". Under it, write one sentence on why your organization needs a plan now.
You can now explain why a nonprofit needs an AI plan and start one from your mission.

check.q: What does an AI plan say?
options: What AI is for, what it is not for, who decides and how you will check it helps
Which AI company to invest in
Only the price of AI tools
check.why: A plan says what AI is for and not for, who decides and how you check it helps the mission.

check.q: A board member asks, "Which AI should we buy?" How do you answer?
options: Start by asking where our team loses time that could go back to the people we serve
check.why: A good plan starts with the mission, not the tool.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Mapping where your team's time goes
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List your organization's repeating tasks and spot the ones AI could help with.
This lesson builds toward: After asking staff and volunteers what eats their week, you will list your repeating tasks and identify which ones AI could help with and which stay with people, keeping every decision about people with people.
AI helps most with tasks that repeat, involve a lot of writing or sorting, and follow a pattern. Examples: weekly volunteer reminders, donor thank-you letters, newsletter drafts, meeting notes, grant report summaries, and answering the same questions from the public.
AI should not make decisions about people: who gets services, who is hired, or who is turned away. Those need human judgment, fairness and care.
Ask three or four people on your team, including a volunteer, what tasks eat their week. You will be surprised what you learn.
Step by step:
- List ten tasks your team does every week or month.
- Next to each, write roughly how many hours it takes.
- Mark tasks that repeat and involve writing, sorting or summarizing.
- Cross out tasks that decide something about a person.
Words to know:
- Repeating task: work done the same way again and again, like weekly reminders.
- Human judgment: decisions a person makes using care, fairness and knowledge of the situation.
Try it now: Make the ten-task list with hours for your organization. Mark the AI-friendly ones and cross out any that decide about people.
You can now map your team's repeating work and pick out tasks that suit AI.

check.q: Which kind of task does AI help with most?
options: Tasks that repeat, involve writing or sorting, and follow a pattern
check.why: AI helps most with repeating, pattern-based writing and sorting tasks.

check.q: Someone suggests using AI to decide which families join the food program. What do you say?
options: Yes, if the AI explains itself
No; decisions about people need human judgment
check.why: AI should not make decisions about who gets services.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Ranking ideas by value and risk
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Rank your AI ideas and choose the top three to start with.
This lesson builds toward: Given your list of AI-friendly tasks, you will score each task from 1 to 3 for value and risk and choose the top three, putting high-value, low-risk tasks first.
For each AI-friendly task, ask two questions. Value: how much time or quality would we gain? Risk: what could go wrong, and how bad would it be?
Low-risk, high-value tasks come first, for example drafting volunteer reminders from public event details. High-risk tasks, like anything with client case notes or health details, wait until you have strong rules and an approved, secure tool, or stay off the list.
Score each from 1 (low) to 3 (high). Start with high value and low risk. Three good tasks are better than ten half-done ones.
Step by step:
- Give each task a value score from 1 to 3.
- Give each task a risk score from 1 to 3.
- Sort: high value and low risk first.
- Pick your top three.
Words to know:
- Value: how much time, money or quality a change would gain.
- Risk: what could go wrong and how much harm it would cause.
Try it now: Score your marked tasks for value and risk. Write your top three under a heading "Where AI will help" in your plan.
You can now rank AI ideas by value and risk and choose three to start with.

check.q: In this lesson, what scale do you use to score value and risk?
You have ten AI ideas. What do you do?
options: Pick about three with high value and low risk
Let each staff member pick one
check.why: Three good tasks are better than ten half-done ones.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing simple AI rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write at least five clear rules for how your staff and volunteers use AI.
This lesson builds toward: For your staff and volunteers, you will write at least five clear rules for using AI, including privacy rules, short enough to fit on one page and simple enough for a new volunteer.
Rules make AI safe to use. Keep them short enough to fit on one page and simple enough for a new volunteer to follow.
Core rules most nonprofits need: use only approved tools; never paste donor, volunteer or client private information; a person reviews everything before it is sent or published; check every fact and number; be honest when AI helped where it matters; and AI never decides who receives services.
Faith-based groups may add a rule about sermons, prayers or pastoral care staying personal. Ask a lawyer or your insurer if you handle health, children's or legal information, because extra laws can apply.
Step by step:
- List the approved AI tools.
- Write the privacy rule: what never goes into AI.
- Write the review rule: who checks before anything goes out.
- Write the decisions rule: AI never decides about people.
- Add any rules your mission needs.
Words to know:
- AI use policy: written rules for how people in your organization may use AI.
- Approved tool: an AI tool your leaders have checked and allowed.
Try it now: Write at least five rules under a heading "Our AI rules" in your plan. Read them to one volunteer and ask if anything is unclear.
You can now write a simple AI use policy your team can follow.

check.q: How long should your AI rules be?
options: Short enough to fit on one page
check.why: Keep rules short enough for one page and simple for a new volunteer.

check.q: Your church wants a rule about prayers and sermons. What could it say?
options: AI chooses who gets prayer visits
Sermons, prayers and pastoral care stay personal
check.why: Faith-based groups may add a rule that these stay personal.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Planning a 30-day pilot
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a small, 30-day test of AI on one task with one owner.
This lesson builds toward: Given one of your top three tasks, you will plan a 30-day pilot with one tool, one owner, a start date and a baseline, with the baseline measured before you start.
A pilot is a small test before you change everything. Pick one of your top three tasks, one tool, one person in charge, and 30 days.
Before you start, measure how things work today. If volunteer reminders take 3 hours a week, write that down. That is your starting point, or baseline.
Keep notes during the pilot: time spent, problems, and what people said. Use a tool your organization already has if you can, such as the AI built into Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, so you do not add cost.
Step by step:
- Choose one task from your top three.
- Choose one approved tool and one owner.
- Write down the baseline: how long it takes today.
- Set a start date and an end date 30 days later.
- Keep simple weekly notes.
Words to know:
- Pilot: a small, short test before a bigger change.
- Baseline: how something works today, measured before you change it.
- Owner: the one person responsible for the pilot.
Try it now: Under "Our 30-day pilot", write the task, tool, owner, start date, end date and baseline.
You can now plan a 30-day AI pilot with a clear owner and baseline.

check.q: What notes do you keep during a pilot?
options: Time spent, problems and what people said
check.why: Keep notes on time spent, problems and what people said.

check.q: You want to start a pilot on newsletter drafts next week. What do you do first?
options: Write down how long newsletters take today
check.why: Measure how things work today first; that is your baseline.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measuring results and reporting to your board
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose two measures and report pilot results in a short board update.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of the pilot, you will compare two measures with the baseline and write a five-sentence board update, with a clear decision to keep, change or stop.
Pick two measures: one for time or cost (hours saved per week) and one for quality (fewer errors, more volunteer sign-ups, faster replies to the public, or what readers said).
At the end, compare to your baseline. Then decide: keep it, change it, or stop it. Stopping is a fine result; you learned something cheaply.
Report to your board in five sentences: what you tested, what changed, any problems, whether rules were followed, and what you recommend next. Boards care about mission, money, risk and trust.
Step by step:
- Choose one time measure and one quality measure.
- Compare the end of the pilot to your baseline.
- Decide: keep, change or stop.
- Write a five-sentence board update.
Words to know:
- Measure: a number or sign you track to see if something worked.
- Board: the group of people who govern a nonprofit and oversee its leaders.
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page AI plan. Add two measures, then put together all five parts: mission, three tasks, rules, the 30-day pilot and the measures you will report to your board.
You can now write a complete one-page AI plan and report results to your board.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Mission first No mission sentence, or the plan starts from a tool. The mission in one sentence opens the plan. Each chosen task says how it gives time back to the mission. Three ranked tasks Tasks are not ranked, or a high-risk task is first. Three tasks scored for value and risk, high value and low risk first. Notes which tasks were left off and why. Clear AI rules Fewer than five rules, or no privacy rule. At least five short rules, including privacy, approved tools and human review. Adds rules for the organization's special risks, such as children's information. 30-day pilot No owner, tool or start date. One task, one tool, one owner, a start date and a measured baseline. Uses a tool the organization already has, with a note on cost. Measures for the board No measures, or measures cannot be compared with the baseline. One time or cost measure and one quality measure. Includes a draft of the five-sentence board update. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a time or cost measure?
check.why: Hours saved per week measures time; the others measure quality.

check.q: The pilot saved time but staff broke a privacy rule once. What goes in the board update?
options: Nothing; it was a small mistake
A request for more money only
The results, the problem, whether rules were followed and what you recommend next
check.why: The update covers what you tested, what changed, problems, rules followed and next steps.
